items.title: PEAK: a phenotype-based classification of genetic variants.
items.abstract: Current variant classifications do not capture clinical severity relative to other pathogenic variants in the same gene. We propose phenotype-exceeding-(mono)allelic-knockout (PEAK) as a term for variants associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than that of heterozygous null alleles. This mechanism-independent designation may facilitate genotype-phenotype interpretation and identify candidates for allele-selective therapeutic development.

Amplification of interferon-γ-driven proinflammatory macrophage responses by granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor: Implications for colorectal cancer immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages in colorectal cancer predominantly exhibit an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype that contributes to tumor progression and resistance to immune checkpoint inhibition. Repolarizing M2 macrophages toward a proinflammatory M1 phenotype represents a promising immunotherapeutic strategy. While interferon-γ promotes M1 macrophage activation, the effect of combining interferon-γ with granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor remains underexplored. THP-1-derived M2-like macrophages were treated with interferon-γ (0-500 ng/mL) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (0-1,000 ng/mL) in a dose-matrix experiment (n = 4). M1 and M2 markers and programmed cell death-ligand 1 were quantified by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction at 24 hours. Secreted interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-α, and interleukin-10 were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. HT-29 colorectal cancer cells were treated with macrophage-conditioned media and assessed for E-cadherin, N-cadherin, vimentin, and Ki-67. Statistical analyses included t tests and analysis of variance. Interferon-γ strongly induced M1 gene expression, whereas granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor alone demonstrated modest effects. Combined interferon-γ (50 ng/mL) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (500 ng/mL) amplified interleukin-6, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10, and tumor necrosis factor-α gene expression 5.4-fold, 2.9-fold, and 3.1-fold, respectively, beyond interferon-γ alone. Two-way analysis of variance showed no significant interaction, suggesting additive rather than synergistic enhancement. Combination treatment increased the secretion of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α and reduced interleukin-10. Conditioned media from combination-treated macrophages increased E-cadherin and reduced N-cadherin, vimentin, and Ki-67 in HT-29 cells. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor augments interferon-γ-driven proinflammatory macrophage responses with protein-level changes and functional effects on colorectal cancer cells. The resulting macrophage secretome was associated with a less mesenchymal, less proliferative colorectal cancer-cell phenotype. Concurrent programmed cell death-ligand 1 upregulation provides a preclinical rationale for evaluating cytokine-mediated macrophage reprogramming in combination with programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death-ligand 1 checkpoint blockade in colorectal cancer.

items.title: Bispecific antibodies in NSCLC: immune reengineering to neutralize adaptive tumor resistance.
items.abstract: Over the past few decades, the emergence of immunotherapy and single-target drugs has brought new promise to the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Yet the high heterogeneity of NSCLC leads to both primary and acquired resistance that neither sequential monotherapy nor empirical combinations can effectively overcome. In contrast to the conventional coadministration of two separate monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) feature a series of molecular engineering designs that confer inherent synergistic antitumor effects. We propose that a network pharmacology perspective can be adopted to understand the application of BsAbs in NSCLC and to guide their subsequent development.

Harnessing a Light-Activated Ruthenium(II) Complex Self-Delivery Nanoplatform for Tumor-Organelle Cascade-Targeted Immunotherapy via Type II Immunogenic Cell Death.
items.abstract: Immunogenic cell death (ICD) converts immunosuppressive "cold" tumors into immunogenic "hot" ones, yet ICD inducers with precise tumor-organelle cascade targeting and spatiotemporal controllability remain largely unexplored. Herein, we report a self-delivery nanoplatform (ER-Ru NPs) constructed via the self-assembly of well-defined tumor-endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cascade-targeting ruthenium(II) complexes. The intrinsic amphiphilicity enables self-assembly of the ruthenium(II) complexes into stabilized nanoparticles with efficient tumor accumulation properties via biotin-mediated active targeting, without any exogenous carriers. Following cellular internalization, the released ruthenium(II) complex monomer specifically accumulates in the ER to generate a cleaved Ru-H2O anticancer agent and in situ reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon red-light irradiation. The robust ROS burst triggers severe ER stress via activation of the PERK/eIF2α pathway, leading to the release of damage-associated molecular patterns and the type II ICD induction. Notably, this cascade-targeted ICD activation strategy enhances not only tumor specificity but also the immunogenicity of dying tumor cells, achieving effective primary tumor ablation in the 4T1 models and simultaneously suppressing distant tumors through dendritic cell maturation, cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, and memory T-cell generation. This study offers a paradigm for photoactivatable, self-delivery ICD inducers with cascade targeting, holding substantial promise for clinical translation in precision cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Persistence of hepatitis A virus in a hydroponic nutrient solution at different temperatures.
items.abstract: Controlled environment agriculture (CEA) enables year-round production of produce to meet growing consumer demands. However, prevention of microbial contamination is essential. This study assessed the persistence of hepatitis A virus (HAV) over 21 days at 4, 15, 20, and 25 °C in a hydroponic nutrient solution to understand cross-contamination risk. Two-hundred μL of HAV (∼6.5 log PFU/mL) was aseptically inoculated into 1.8 mL of a commercial hydroponic nutrient solution (pH 5.8) and stored at 4, 15, 20, or 25 °C (mimicking storage, transport, and cultivation conditions) for 21 days. Infectious viruses were recovered over time and quantified using plaque assays in duplicate. The obtained recovered virus data from triplicate experiments were statistically analyzed. Hepatitis A virus retained infectivity after 21 days with reductions ranging from 0.22 log PFU/mL to 3.34 log PFU/mL. Storage at 4 °C supported greatest viral persistence (D-value = 41.34 ± 4.06 days), compared to 15 °C (D-value = 9.23 ± 2.70 days), 20 °C (D-value = 6.31 ± 3.92 days) or 25 °C (D-value = 8.03 ± 0.22 days). These findings support the risk associated with the contamination of hydroponic nutrient solutions, as the temperature of the solution shows an impact on the persistence of HAV. Overall, this study emphasized the need for adequate precautions and implementation of control methods in CEA to reduce the risk of foodborne viral cross-contamination.

items.title: High persistence of hepatitis A and E viruses during simulated gastrointestinal digestion across diverse food matrices.
items.abstract: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV) are major causes of foodborne viral infections worldwide. Although both viruses are known to be transmitted via the fecal-oral route, their persistence during passage through the human gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the presence of different food matrices, remains poorly characterized. In this study, the persistence of HAV and HEV was evaluated using two complementary in vitro digestion models, the static INFOGEST 2.0 protocol and the dynamic TIM-1 system, simulating conditions of the stomach and small intestine. Different food matrices associated with viral transmission, including berries, oysters, lettuce (HAV) and pork liver pâté (HEV), were investigated. HAV infectivity was assessed by plaque assays, while HAV and HEV genome were quantified by RT-qPCR following PMAxx pretreatment. For both viruses, viral levels at the end of the digestion were comparable to initial concentration across all tested matrices and in both models. Although minor variations were observed at specific time points, these were not statistically significant. Overall, the results indicate that HAV and HEV exhibit high persistence under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, with limited influence of the food matrix. These findings suggest that intrinsic viral resistance rather than matrix-dependent protection governs their survival during digestion, highlighting a potential risk to consumers even at low contamination levels. This study underscores the need to better account for viral persistence during digestion in food safety risk assessments and control strategies.

Hepatic Cysts in Korea: Prevalence, Incidence, and Risk Factors Based on a 5.8-Year Follow-up Health Screening Cohort.
items.abstract: Hepatic cysts are fluid-filled liver lesions that are mostly asymptomatic, but fewer than 15% of patients present clinically significant symptoms. Reported prevalence ranges from 2.5% to 71%, yet prior studies have been limited by small populations and incomplete assessment of risk factors. This study aimed to determine the prevalence, incidence, and risk factors using data from a large health screening cohort in Korea. We performed a retrospective cohort analysis of 78,676 participants in the Health and Prevention Enhancement cohort who underwent abdominal ultrasound at the Seoul National University Hospital Healthcare System Gangnam Center from 2003 and 2014. Hepatic cysts were identified using a validated rule-based text-mining algorithm applied to ultrasound reports. Prevalence was estimated from baseline data. Incidence was assessed in 41,179 participants initially negative for hepatic cysts. Risk factors were determined through Cox proportional hazards modeling. The prevalence of hepatic cysts at baseline was 8.54% (95% confidence interval [95% CI], 8.34-8.73). The incidence was 23.4 per 1,000 person-years at risk (95% CI, 22.8-24.0). Cox regression identified hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBs-Ag) positivity (hazard ratio [HR], 1.20; 95% CI, 1.00-1.45) and renal cyst presence (HR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.31-1.64) as independent risk factors, whereas diabetes mellitus (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and high physical activity (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.81-0.97) appeared protective. This study provides the prevalence of 8.54%, incidence, and risk factors of hepatic cysts. Renal cyst presence and HBs-Ag positivity are significant risk factors, whereas high physical activity and diabetic status are protective.

items.title: Integrative Target Fishing and Proteomics Reveal the Molecular Targets of Abrus cantoniensis in Alleviating Dyslipidemia.
items.abstract: Abrus cantoniensis (AC) is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used for hepatitis, with demonstrated lipid-regulating activity. However, as a multi-component herbal system, the specific bioactive monomers and their direct protein targets remain to be elucidated. This study integrates target fishing with proteomics to capture hepatic protein targets of AC and elucidate its lipid-regulating mechanisms. Abrine, a pharmacopoeial marker compound employed as a probe, was used to synthesize abrine-functionalized magnetic beads (Fe 3 O 4 -SH-BP-abrine, FSBA) via photo-crosslinking for target capture from mouse liver lysates. Proteins were identified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Bioinformatic analyses, including Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), were conducted. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), immunohistochemistry (IHC), and Western blotting (WB) were employed for validation. AC ameliorated hepatic steatosis in HFD-induced dyslipidemic mice. KEGG enrichment identified the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) as the top-ranked pathway, consistent with its central role in NADPH-dependent lipid biosynthesis. Molecular docking and MD simulations predicted stable interactions between abrine and PPP enzymes. SPR verified a direct interaction between abrine and G6PD. RT-qPCR demonstrated downregulation of G6pd, Tkt, Taldo1, H6pd, and Aldoa at the mRNA level. IHC and WB consistently showed reduced protein expression of G6PD, PGD, and TKT after AC treatment. Target fishing combined with proteomics uncovered AC's anti-dyslipidemic mechanism via the PPP. The identified PPP-related targets provide mechanistic insight into AC's lipid-regulating activity.

LRH-1 is a novel regulator of neutrophil-driven immune responses within the tumor microenvironment.
items.abstract: Plasma cholesterol is correlated with worse outcomes in breast and ovarian cancer. Prior work indicates that myeloid immune cells are highly responsive to cholesterol metabolism. Interestingly, Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (LRH-1, or NR5A2), a key transcriptional regulator of cholesterol homeostasis is highly expressed in neutrophils and is associated with increased survival time. However, the roles of LRH-1 within neutrophils remain unclear. We therefore focused on how LRH-1 influences neutrophil behaviors relevant to cancer. Small molecule ligands for LRH-1 regulated neutrophil migration towards cancer cells. Phagocytosis was also regulated by LRH-1 ligands, the extent being dependent on type of bait (e. coli vs. cancer cells). In T cell co-cultures, neutrophils pretreated with an LRH-1 agonist promoted greater T cell expansion, particularly in CD4 + cells, while LRH-1 inhibition suppressed this response. NETosis is a known trigger of recurrence from dormancy and subsequent tumor growth. Importantly LRH-1 activation reduced NETosis, while treatment with an antagonist or inverse agonist enhanced NETosis, likely through altered reactive oxygen species. Treatment of mice with an inverse agonist of LRH-1 increased the growth of mammary tumors in a NET-dependent manner. Mice harboring dormant D2.0R mammary cancer lesions treated with an LRH-1 inverse agonist exhibited earlier tumor recurrence and enhanced metastatic progression. In contrast, treatment with BL001, a small chemical LRH-1 agonist, delayed recurrence in D2.0R-grafted mice. These findings reveal that LRH-1 is a novel regulator of neutrophil-driven immune responses within the tumor microenvironment. LRH-1 is thus a promising therapeutic target to suppress the progression of breast and ovarian cancer.

items.title: Epidemiological comparison of cirrhosis to other long-term health conditions in the United Kingdom.
items.abstract: Although cirrhosis is a serious long-term health condition (LTC), it tends to receive little attention from healthcare policymakers. Here, we sought to describe how cirrhosis compares to other LTCs to inform priority-setting discussions. We analysed data from the Our Future Health (OFH) study, a cohort of ∼1.7 million individuals from England, United Kingdom. Self-reported diagnosis status for cirrhosis and 15 benchmark LTCs (including type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease, chronic kidney disease, schizophrenia, and stage 4 cancer) were ascertained from the enrolment questionnaire. Each LTC was profiled with respect to: sociodemographic characteristics; mortality; comorbidity burden; and late diagnosis. Furthermore, information on each LTC's trajectory (i.e., increasing, stable, or decreasing over time) was determined from background mortality data over the last decade. The study cohort included 1,613,777 participants, of whom 2,606 (0.2%) reported a diagnosis of cirrhosis. Mortality elevation for participants with cirrhosis versus without was substantial (HR: 7.46; P<0.001, with adjustment for age/sex) and comparable to dementia (HR:7.60), stage 4 cancer (HR:7.06), whilst higher than schizophrenia (HR:4.46) and heart failure (HR:4.01). People with cirrhosis had more co-existing health conditions/diseases than other LTCs (i.e., elevated prevalence for 58/145 distinct health conditions; second only to stage 4 cancer). Area-based deprivation score was third highest for cirrhosis, behind COPD and schizophrenia. Late diagnosis of cirrhosis was commonplace, with <15% of new-onset liver failure reporting cirrhosis at enrolment. Cirrhosis also exhibited an upward trajectory, with mortality increasing by ∼20% in the last decade. Cirrhosis is an anomaly LTC with respect to its deprivation, comorbidity, mortality, upward trajectory, and late diagnosis profile. Our data provide comparative evidence to inform priority-setting discussions with policymakers. Various levers are available to policy makers for reducing incidence of liver cirrhosis. However, other health conditions are often prioritised by policy makers ahead of cirrhosis; the decision-making process around this is not always transparent nor grounded in evidence. This study explores the characteristics of cirrhosis relative to other long-term conditions through a public-health lens. Our findings may guide priority-setting discussions between policy makers, advocates and other stakeholders and may shift current discourse onto a more empirical footing.

items.title: Dosimetric impact of baseline shift plan in a magnetic resonance linear accelerator according to target motion and plan characteristics.
items.abstract: In this study, the dosimetric effect of baseline shift (BLS) in a magnetic resonance linear accelerator was investigated and compared with adapt-to-position (ATP), adapt-to-shape (ATS), and an uncorrected plan without adaptation. In a simulation dataset consisting of 30 patients (10 prostate, 10 liver, 10 pancreatic), all structures were rigidly shifted by 1, 3, 5, and 10 mm separately in the superior-inferior and posterior directions, and four plans (ATS reoptimization, ATP reoptimization, BLS using the segment aperture morphing algorithm, and an uncorrected plan without adaptation) were generated for each shift condition. Planning target volume (PTV) coverage and PTV maximum dose (Dmax) were then compared. The dosimetric effects of BLS on the targets and organs at risk (OARs) under non-rigid anatomic changes were also evaluated using a clinical dataset based on magnetic resonance imaging acquired during treatment. In the simulation analysis of superior-inferior shifts, target coverage using BLS was comparable to that using ATS and ATP across all disease sites and improved compared with that using the uncorrected plan. For posterior shifts, target coverage remained comparable to that using ATS and ATP; however, BLS increased the PTV Dmax at all posterior shift magnitudes (1-10 mm) in prostate and pancreatic cases, with limited increases in liver cases. In the clinical dataset, OAR doses upon left-right or anterior-posterior displacement were greater using BLS than using ATP, ATS, and uncorrected plans in the prostate and pancreatic cases, with limited increases in the liver cases. The dosimetric impact of BLS relies on motion direction and plan characteristics. BLS was stable for superior-inferior shifts, whereas posterior shifts may increase PTV hotspots and OAR doses. Therefore, clinical application of BLS should consider motion direction and plan design rather than applying a uniform strategy.

items.title: Site-Specific Outcomes and Genomics in Metastatic Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.abstract: Clinical and molecular features of pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) according to involved metastatic sites have not been well characterized. We used the Foundry platform to query information for patients with metastatic PDAC at MD Anderson Cancer Center. Involved metastatic sites were extracted using natural language processing from imaging reports and verified by chart reviews. Overall survival (OS) and next generation sequencing (NGS) data were analyzed. In a cohort of 1,095 patients (median overall survival [OS]: 22.8 months), lung-only metastasis was associated with longer median OS (57.6 months, p<0.0001). Patients with metastases not involving the liver had OS of 41.3 months, while liver-only (19.5 months) and multiple sites including liver (19.3 months) had the poorest survival. TP53 mutation rates were higher in liver-involved groups (84-85%) versus lung-only (73%) and non-liver metastases (67%, p<0.0001). Lower rates of GNAS mutations were detected in liver-only (5%) and liver-involved (2%) cases, higher in lung-only (8%) and non-liver (10%, p<0.01). The frequency of KRAS mutation and mutant allele distribution were not significantly different in tissue based NGS. However, in liquid biopsy analysis (n = 240), lung-only metastasis showed the lowest mutation detection (50%), TP53 (23%) and KRAS (10%), compared to liver-only detection rates of 65%, 46%, and 52% respectively (p values: 0.009, 0.02, <0.001). Patients with PDAC without liver metastasis have significantly improved OS and lower rates of TP53 mutation. Patients with lung-only metastasis had longer OS, a lower liquid-biopsy positivity rate, and a lower rate of KRAS detection by liquid biopsy; because liquid biopsy may under-detect KRAS in lung-only disease, tumor-tissue sequencing should be prioritized in these patients as KRAS-directed therapies emerge.
